title: Velvet Ant
summary: Velvet Ant is a China linked intrusion set that public reporting describes as targeting telecommunications providers and network infrastructure, with a focus on holding access quietly rather than disrupting operations. Reporting has described compromises of network appliances and the reuse of surviving embedded services to reach into internal networks. The group is also associated with long term persistence and with a tendency to reuse credentials and tooling across campaigns, which makes separate incidents look related. Tradecraft includes living off the land activity, such as using built in networking utilities to tunnel traffic and avoid obvious malware. Attribution is limited: public reporting ties the activity to China with moderate confidence based on target selection, infrastructure and shared tooling, and does not identify named individuals. Evidence sits mainly in device and network logs rather than on monitored workstations.

beginner.definition: Velvet Ant is a team of intruders that stays inside networks for a long time. Public reports link this group to China. They often work on network equipment, such as routers and switches, instead of normal office computers.
beginner.whyItMatters: Network equipment is easy to forget. Nobody installs office software on a switch. If an intruder lives there, they can watch traffic and reach many systems at once. They also survive password changes on laptops, because they hold their own access. This is why quiet, patient intrusions are so difficult to remove.
howItWorks: They find a network device that is exposed and rarely checked.
They use a stolen or default administrator password to log in.
They add their own access so it survives a restart or a cleanup.
They use tools that are already on the device, so nothing looks new.
They tunnel traffic through it to reach computers further inside.
They stay quiet, watch for a long time, and tell nobody what they find.
beginner.example: Think of the small electrical cupboard in an office corridor. Nobody looks inside it for years. Someone hides there with a chair and a notebook, listening to every conversation that passes the door. Changing the office door locks does not bother him, because he never used the front door.
takeaways: Network devices need updates, strong passwords and logging too.
An attacker who avoids malware is hard to spot with antivirus alone.
Device logs from routers and switches are often the only evidence you get.

objectives: Explain why managed network devices are attractive long term footholds for intruders.
Describe living off the land behaviour and why it evades signature based detection.
Outline a basic hardening checklist for network appliances including logging and credentials.
Explain how tunnelling through a trusted device helps an intruder reach internal systems.
Discuss why public attribution of this cluster is limited and moderately confident.
